The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,
$$\int_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}h(\theta,x)\,J(d\theta,dx)=\int_\Theta\left(\int_\mathcal Xh(\theta,x)\,K(\theta,dx)\right)\pi(d\theta).$$
In particular, $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$ for
$A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal A$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Assume AC. Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable random element with standard-Borel target, and let $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be any sub-sigma-algebra. There exists a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\mathcal G$. Every section is a probability measure, including at exceptional sample points, and no countable-generation or completeness assumption on $\mathcal G$ is required.

For this necessarily nonempty target, the construction also supplies a bimeasurable bijection $c:E\to B$ onto a Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$, and a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ which generates $\mathcal S$, separates points, and determines finite measures.

Let a proper Bayesian model be given, and let $J$ be its joint prior-predictive probability on $(\Theta\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal Y)$, supplied by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. More generally, let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,Q)$ be any probability space carrying parameter and data random elements $X:\Omega\to\Theta$ and $Y:\Omega\to\mathsf Y$ whose joint law is $J$ ([[def-probability-measure]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). A **posterior regular conditional distribution (posterior RCD)** is a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$, in the sense of [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. It is a kernel indexed by the sample point $\omega\in\Omega$. The canonical realization is $\Omega=\Theta\times\mathsf Y$ with $Q=J$ and coordinate maps $X(\theta,y)=\theta$, $Y(\theta,y)=y$.

A **data-indexed posterior kernel** is a probability kernel $\Pi_{\cdot}$ from $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ to $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) for which $\omega\mapsto\Pi_{Y(\omega)}$ is a conditional law of $X$ given $Y$ ([[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]). Equivalently, for every $A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$,
$$Q(X\in A,\ Y\in B)=\int_B\Pi_y(A)\,Q_Y(dy),$$
where $Q_Y$ is the data marginal (equal to $J_Y$). This kernel is indexed by data values, not sample points.

The definition asserts no existence of either conditional kernel. Values of a data-indexed version on a measurable $J_Y$-null set are not fixed by the conditional-law identities; replacing them there by a fixed probability preserves those identities. A dominated-density construction is a separate route: [[thm-bayes-formula-for-dominated-kernels]] requires a proper prior, a sigma-finite data measure, and a specified jointly measurable sampling density, and fills fibres whose marginal density is zero or infinite with the prior. It does not require the data space to be standard Borel.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the model's prior and sampling kernel define the joint probability $J$ on the canonical product space. The given random elements $X,Y$ have this same joint law, and [F2] supplies the random-element and pushforward-law meanings used for this realization.

The target $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ is standard Borel and AC is assumed. Apply [F3] to $(\Omega,\mathcal F,Q)$, the given random element $X$, and the sub-sigma-algebra $\mathcal G=\sigma(Y)$. It gives an RCD of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$; by [F4] this is the stated posterior RCD. The RCD theorem places no standard-Borel condition on $\mathsf Y$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,
$$\int_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}h(\theta,x)\,J(d\theta,dx)=\int_\Theta\left(\int_\mathcal Xh(\theta,x)\,K(\theta,dx)\right)\pi(d\theta).$$
In particular, $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$ for
$A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal A$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let a proper Bayesian model have joint prior-predictive law $J$, and let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,Q)$ be any probability space carrying parameter and data random elements $X,Y$ whose joint law is $J$ ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). If $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ is standard Borel ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), then a posterior RCD of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$ exists. The data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ need only be measurable. In particular, the claim applies to the canonical product realization supplied by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]].

Assume AC. Let $X$ and $Y$ take values in nonempty standard-Borel spaces $(E,\mathcal S)$ and $(T,\mathcal T)$ on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$. Let $L$ be a specified regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$, everywhere a probability kernel. There is a probability kernel $K:T\to E$ such that $L(\omega,\cdot)=K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ simultaneously outside a single null set. In fact, with the stated everywhere-kernel convention, the construction below gives this equality for every $\omega$. Consequently K is a conditional law of X given Y.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ and $Y:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\mathcal T)$ be measurable random elements. A **conditional law of X given Y** is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that $\omega\mapsto K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$ in [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. Thus for every $A\in\mathcal S$ and $H\in\sigma(Y)$,
$$\int_H K(Y(\omega),A)\,dP=P(H\cap\{X\in A\}).$$

Composition with Y makes each evaluation $\sigma(Y)$-measurable, and every section remains a probability by [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. The notation $P(X\in A\mid Y=y)=K(y,A)$ refers to a chosen kernel; it is not a ratio involving the possibly zero probability $P(Y=y)$.

Write $P_Y(B)=P(Y^{-1}(B))$ for the law in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. If a specified countable family $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S$ determines probability measures, two conditional laws K,L agree as measures outside a single $\mathcal T$-measurable $P_Y$-null set. Indeed for each $A\in\mathcal C$ the measurable discrepancy $D_A=\{y:K(y,A)\ne L(y,A)\}$ has null inverse image under Y by [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]]. Hence $P_Y(D_A)=0$ by the law definition; the countable union $D$ is null by [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]], and off D the determining property gives equality of measures. This uses a supplied determining family and makes no AC assertion about obtaining one.

Values on a measurable $P_Y$-null subset may be replaced by a specified fixed probability on E without changing these identities. The inverse image of that subset is measurable null, and all event evaluations are bounded, so the modified event integrals agree. Empty-event evaluations remain zero and whole-target evaluations remain one. Existence on standard-Borel spaces is proved separately; the definition alone does not assert a conditional kernel exists.

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $J$ is a probability measure on $(\Theta\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal Y)$ and $J_Y(B)=J(\Theta\times B)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,B)\,\Pi(d\theta)$. Its coordinate maps $X$ and $Y$ are measurable by [F2].
Since $\Theta$ is standard Borel and [A1] holds, [F3] supplies a posterior RCD $L$ of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$ on the canonical space of step 1.1.

Both $\Theta$ and $\mathsf Y$ are standard Borel and [A1] holds, so [F4] factors $L$ through $Y$ as a probability kernel $\Pi_y$; hence its evaluations are $\mathcal Y$-measurable and every section is a probability. By [F5], the composition $\Pi_Y$ is a posterior RCD, with rectangle identity $J(A\times B)=\int_B\Pi_y(A)\,J_Y(dy)$.

Apply [F6] to the same joint probability $J$. It gives uniqueness of the disintegration kernel as a probability measure outside one $J_Y$-null set. Replacing a version on any measurable $J_Y$-null set by the prior $\Pi$ preserves every rectangle identity, as [F5] records. Thus the conditional identities alone do not choose a pointwise value there; each section must still be a probability measure.

let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,
$$\int_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}h(\theta,x)\,J(d\theta,dx)=\int_\Theta\left(\int_\mathcal Xh(\theta,x)\,K(\theta,dx)\right)\pi(d\theta).$$
In particular, $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$ for
$A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal A$.

derivations.claim: The joint law assigns mass $3/8$ to each diagonal point $(0,0),(1,1)$ and $1/8$ to each off-diagonal point; hence $J_Y(0)=J_Y(1)=1/2$.

For each $y$, $\Pi_y$ has masses $3/4$ at $y$ and $1/4$ at $1-y$, so it is a probability, with $\Pi_y(\{y\})J_Y(y)=3/8=J(y,y)$ and $\Pi_y(\{1-y\})J_Y(y)=1/8=J(1-y,y)$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let
$$\mathsf E=((\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Equip the parameter set with a specified measurable structure $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **proper Bayesian model** based on this experiment consists of a prior probability measure $\Pi$ on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]) and a probability kernel $K$ from $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) that represents the experiment:
$$K(\theta,B)=P_\theta(B)\qquad(\theta\in\Theta,\ B\in\mathcal Y).$$
Thus $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,B)$ is $\mathcal T$-measurable for every data event $B$, as required for a parameter-measurable model ([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). The family of measures in a parametric model alone does not supply this parameter sigma-algebra or measurability condition ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

It does not require the data space to be standard Borel.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). In a proper Bayesian model, suppose both parameter and data spaces $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ are standard Borel ([[def-standard-borel-space]]). Let $J$ be the joint prior-predictive law and let $J_Y$ be its data marginal. There is a data-indexed posterior probability kernel $y\mapsto\Pi_y$ such that, for all $A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$,
$$J(A\times B)=\int_B\Pi_y(A)\,J_Y(dy),\qquad J_Y(B)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,B)\,\Pi(d\theta).$$
The composition $\Pi_{Y(\omega)}$ is a posterior RCD. Any two data-indexed posterior kernels agree as probability measures outside one measurable $J_Y$-null set. On any measurable $J_Y$-null set, the conditional-law identities do not select a pointwise value: replacing the kernel there by the prior $\Pi$ preserves the identities.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

derivations.claim: The discrete metric on $\mathbb N_0$ is complete because every Cauchy sequence is eventually constant; $\mathbb N_0$ itself is a countable dense subset. Its topology is discrete, so its Borel sigma-algebra is the power set. The finite discrete parameter space has the same properties. Thus both spaces are standard Borel by [F5]–[F6]. By [F4], $\sum_nf_0(n)=1$ and $\sum_nf_1(n)=1$, so they define probability sampling laws and the prior in [F1] gives a Bayesian model.

Since both spaces are standard Borel and AC holds, [F3] supplies a data-indexed posterior kernel. For every $n$, both $f_0(n)$ and $f_1(n)$ are positive and finite, so $m(n)>0$ and the displayed values are in $[0,1]$ and sum to one. Every function on the discrete data space is measurable, hence $n\mapsto\Pi_n$ is a probability kernel.

For $i\in\{0,1\}$ and every $B\subseteq\mathbb N_0$, $\sum_{n\in B}\Pi_n(i)m(n)=\frac12\sum_{n\in B}f_i(n)=J(\{i\}\times B)$. Adding the identities for $i=0,1$ proves the rectangle identity for every $A\subseteq\Theta$ and every data event $B$. Thus the explicit kernel is a data-indexed posterior version; all its data values have positive prior-predictive mass.

Let $\pi$ be a prior probability on $(E,\mathcal S)$ and let $Q:E\to T$ be a probability kernel dominated by a sigma-finite measure $\nu$ on $(T,\mathcal T)$, with specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $\ell:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$:
$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

The observation marginal is $m\,d\nu$, and the filled fibres have marginal mass zero. This is a choice-free assertion about the explicit kernel and event identities.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Assigning mass $1/3$ to each disjoint atom defines a probability measure $\nu$: a pairwise disjoint family has at most three nonempty members, so countable additivity reduces to finite additivity on the atoms. Let $d$ be a compatible metric. For every $z\ne h(u)$, the ball about $z$ of radius $d(z,h(u))/2$ misses $h(u)$, so $\{h(u)\}$ is closed and Borel. Its inverse image under $h$ would be a measurable set separating $u$ and $u'$, a contradiction.

u= rac32\cdot rac23=1$ and $\int f_1\,d
u=3\cdot rac13=1$. Thus the sections define sampling probabilities, and the finite reference measure $
